opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core intuition is that the running agent has context that no outside agent can easily reconstruct. When an agent is in the middle of a task, it's accumulated all this state: it knows which tool calls failed, where it got confused, which parts of its own prompt or scaffolding were actually load-bearing and which were just noise. It has felt the friction firsthand, so to speak. A separate agent coming in to modify it is basically doing archaeology. It's reading logs or traces after the fact and trying to infer what went wrong, and a lot of that signal gets lost in translation.

The second piece is the tightness of the loop. If the agent can modify itself while it's running, say by rewriting a tool, adjusting its own instructions, or adding a helper function, it can immediately test that change against the exact situation that motivated it. You get this really fast cycle of noticing a problem, patching it, and checking whether the patch helped, all within one trajectory. With an external modifier you usually have a batch process: run the agent, collect failures, hand them to an optimizer, deploy a new version, run again. That's much slower and much coarser.

And then, honestly, there's a compounding argument. An agent that improves itself in-flight can turn the improved version on the next sub-problem right away, and that improved version may be better at spotting the next thing to fix. You get a kind of bootstrapping that's hard to replicate when improvement is always mediated by some other process sitting outside the loop.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are real risks: drift, the agent breaking itself, reward hacking its own evaluation, and it's harder to audit. So in practice you want guardrails, like versioning, the ability to roll back, and some external check on whether a self-modification actually helped. But in terms of raw capability, the agent that's living through the problem is just in a much better position to fix it than someone looking over its shoulder afterward.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts self-modification with an outside modifier, but does not say that using the outside agent still requires trusting the machine making the changes.

r002.rationale: It says the running agent knows which tool calls failed and where it got confused, and can use that firsthand runtime context to guide and test changes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition most people have is the opposite, right? You'd think the cleaner design is: you have an agent doing a task, and then you have some separate thing watching it, and that thing decides when to tweak the prompt, or add a tool, or change the scaffold. Separation of concerns. That feels safer and more principled.

But the problem is that the outside agent is always working from a lossy picture. It sees traces, it sees the final outputs, maybe it sees some metrics. What it doesn't have is the actual state of being stuck in the middle of the task. Like, the moment where the running agent goes, "I've called this tool three times and the output format is useless to me," or "I keep having to re-derive this one piece of context every turn." That's the signal that matters, and it's richest right at the point where it's happening. By the time you've exported it out to some separate process and it's reading logs, a lot of that is gone or flattened.

So when the running agent can modify itself, you close that loop really tight. It notices the friction, it changes the thing, and it immediately gets to test whether the change helped, because it's still in the middle of the task it was trying to do. The feedback is basically free. With a separate agent, you have to go through a whole cycle: collect traces, propose a change, redeploy, run more tasks, see if the metric moved. That's a much slower and noisier gradient.

There's also a weird thing where the separate agent is sort of the same model anyway. So you're not actually getting a smarter overseer, you're getting the same intelligence with less context. If the argument for separation is "a fresh set of eyes," fine, but you can get a fresh set of eyes from within the running agent too, just spin up a sub-call that looks at the current state. You don't have to give up the context to get the perspective.

Now, I want to be fair: the reason people reach for the separate agent is control. If the thing can rewrite its own tools and its own instructions, it can also wander off and optimize for the wrong thing, or just break itself. And that's real. But I'd frame that as a problem of what it's allowed to modify and how you check the changes, not a reason to pull the modification out of the loop entirely. You can let it edit its own tools, version everything, and have a cheap check on whether the task is still getting done. That gets you most of the power without most of the downside. Whereas if you start from the separate-agent design, you've thrown away the power up front and you're never really getting it back.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risks and safeguards for self-modification, but does not state that a separate modifying agent still requires trusting the machine making the changes.

r002.rationale: It says the running agent can notice task friction in the moment—such as repeated useless tool calls or context it keeps re-deriving—and use that signal to change its design.

astra-6.text:
I think the advantage is that the running agent has the context of what it’s trying to do and where it’s getting stuck. If I’m in the middle of a task and realize, “The tool I have doesn’t expose the thing I need,” I can make that change and immediately try it against the problem that motivated it.

A separate agent can modify the same code, but you have to transfer that context: what failed, why it matters, what success would look like. The running agent already has that in its trajectory. So you get a tighter feedback loop between doing the work, improving the system, and seeing whether the improvement actually helps.

It’s not that a separate agent couldn’t do it. It’s that self-modification makes improving how you work part of doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says a separate agent requires transferring context about failures and success, but does not say that it still requires trusting the machine making the changes.

r002.rationale: The response describes the running agent using its task context and noticing where it gets stuck, but does not identify runtime inspection as evidence guiding its design changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the running agent has context about what it’s trying to do and where it’s getting stuck. A separate agent can inspect the code and make improvements, but it has to reconstruct that context. The agent doing the work can say, “I’ve tried this three times, and the reason it keeps failing is that my tools don’t let me do this particular thing. Let me change that.”

So you get this much tighter feedback loop between encountering a limitation, modifying the system, and seeing whether the change actually helps. It’s not that a separate agent can’t do it. It’s that the agent experiencing the problem has a lot of information about what needs to change, and self-modification lets it act on that information directly.

r001.rationale: The response compares the running agent with a separate agent but does not say that using the separate agent requires trusting the machine making changes.

r002.rationale: It says the running agent can use its own experience—what it has tried and where its tools fail—to identify changes, then observe whether those changes help.
